source_text: Video jam hinc ad Apostolum nos provocari. Ad cujus sensum facilius perspiciendum, tanto instantius praeculcandum est mulierum magis defuncto marito teneri, quominus alium virum admittat. Recogitemus enim repudium, aut discordia fieri, aut discordiam facere; mortem vero ex lege Dei, non ex hominis offensa evenire. Idque omnium esse debitum, etiam non maritorum. Igitur si repudiata quae per discordiam, et iram, et odium, et caussas eorum, injuriam vel contumeliam, vel quamlibet querelam, et anima et corpore separata est, tenetur inimico, ne dicam marito; quanto magis, illa, quae neque suo, neque mariti vitio, sed dominicae legis eventu, a matrimonio non separata, sed relicta, ejus erit etiam defuncti, cui etiam defuncto concordiam debet! A quo repudium non audiit, non divertit; cui repudium nn scripsit, cum ipso est; quem amisisse noluit, retinet. Habet secum animi licentiam, qui omnia homini quae non habet, imaginario fructu repraesentat. Ipsam denique interrogo foeminam: Dic mihi, soror, in pace praemisisti virum tuum? Quid respondebit? An in discordia? Ergo hoc magis ei vincta est, cum quo habet apud Deum caussam. Non discessit, quae tenetur. Sed in pace. Ergo perseveret in ea cum illo necesse est, quem jam repudiare non poterit, ne sic quidem nuptura si repudiare potuisset. Enim vero et pro anima ejus orat, et refrigerium interim adpostulat ei, et in prima resurrectione consortium, et offert annuis diebus dormitionis ejus. Nam haec nisi fecerit, vere repudiavit, quantum in ipsa est; et quidem hoc iniquius, quanto quo modo potuit, quia non potuit; et hoc indignius, quanto jam indignius, si quia non meruit. Aut numquid nihil crimus post mortem? Secundum aliquem Epicurum, et non secundum Christum. Quod si credimus mortuorum resurrectionem, utique tenebimur, cum quibus resurrecturi sumus, rationem de alterutro reddituri. Si autem in illo aevo neque nubent neque nubentur, sed erunt aequales angelis; non ideo non tenebitur conjugibus defunctis, quia non erit restitutio conjugii. Atquin eo magis tenebimur, quia in meliorem statum destinamur, resurrecturi in spiritale consortium, agnituri tam nosmetipsos, quam et nostros. Caeterum, quomodo gratias Deo in aeternum canemus, si non manebit in nobis sensus et memoria debiti hujus? si substantia, non conscientia reformabimur? Ergo qui cum Deo erimus, simul erimus, dum omnes apud Deum unum (licet merces varia, licet. multae mansiones penes patrem eumdem) uno denario ejusdem mercedis operati, id est vitae aeternae, in qua magis non separabit quos conjunxit Deus, quam in ista minore vita separari vetat. Cum haec ita sint, quomodo alii viro vacabit, quae suo etiam in futurum occupata est? Utrique autem sexui loquimur, etsi ad alterum sermo est; quia una disciplina praeest. Alium habebit in spiritu, alium in carne? Hoc erit adulterium, unius foeminae in duos viros conscientia. Si alter a carne disjunctus est, sed in corde remanet; illic (ubi etiam cogitatus sine carnis congressu, et adulterium ante perficit ex concupiscentia, et matrimonium ex voluntate) usque adhuc maritus est, ipsum illud possidens, per quod et factus est, id est animum: in quo si et alius habitabit, hoc erit crimen. Caeterum, non est exclusus, si a viliore commercio carnis decessit. Honoratior maritus est, quando mundior factus est.
pass_a_gloss: I see that we are now being summoned to the Apostle. To whose sense, in order that it may be more easily understood, it must be more urgently trampled down that women, with their husband having died, are held back from admitting another man. For let us consider that divorce happens, or discord is made, or discord is caused; but death indeed happens from the law of God, not from a man's offense. And this is a debt of all, even of those not married. Therefore, if she who has been divorced on account of discord, and anger, and hatred, and the causes of these, injury or insult, or any complaint, is separated in soul and body, she is held to her enemy, I do not say her husband; how much more so will she be, who, neither by her own fault nor her husband's, but by the outcome of the Lord's law, is not separated from marriage, but left, and will be her husband's even when he is dead, to whom she owes concord even when he is dead. From whom she has not heard a divorce, she has not been turned away; to whom a divorce was not written, she is with him; whom she did not want to lose, she retains. She has with her the freedom of her mind, which represents to a man all that he does not have with an imaginary fruit. Finally, I ask the woman herself: Tell me, sister, did you send your husband ahead in peace? What will she respond? Or in discord? Therefore, she is bound to him all the more, with whom she has a case before God. She who is held back does not depart. But in peace. Therefore, she must persevere in it with him, since she cannot repudiate him now, not even if she were to marry, if she could repudiate him. For indeed she also prays for his soul, and demands refreshment for him in the meantime, and consortium in the first resurrection, and offers on the annual days of his death. For if she does not do these things, she has truly repudiated him, as far as it is in her; and indeed this is more unjust, inasmuch as she could not, because she could not; and this is more unworthy, inasmuch as it is now more unworthy, if she did not deserve it. Or do we think that we will be nothing after death, according to some Epicurean, and not according to Christ? But if we believe in the resurrection of the dead, we will certainly be held to account, with those with whom we will be resurrected, to render an account of each other. But if in that age they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be equal to angels, this does not mean that we will not be held to our deceased spouses, because there will not be a restoration of marriage. On the contrary, we will be held all the more, because we are destined for a better state, to be resurrected into a spiritual consortium, recognizing both ourselves and our own. Moreover, how will we sing thanks to God in eternity, if the sense and memory of this debt do not remain in us, if we are reformed in substance, not in conscience? Therefore, when we are with God, we will be together, while all of us, with God, are one (although the rewards are varied, although there are many dwellings with the same Father), having worked for the same wage, that is, eternal life, in which God will not separate those whom He has joined more than He forbids separation in this lesser life. Since these things are so, how will she be free for another man, who is occupied with her own even in the future? We speak to both sexes, although the speech is to one; because one discipline is in charge. Will she have another in spirit, another in flesh? This will be adultery, the conscience of one woman with two men. If another is separated from the flesh, but remains in the heart, there (where even a thought without fleshly union, and adultery is perfected from desire, and marriage from will), he is still a husband, possessing that by which he was also made, that is, the mind: in which, if another dwells, this will be a crime. Moreover, he is not excluded, if he has departed from a lesser commerce of the flesh. The husband is more honored when he has been made purer.

pass_b_english: I see we are now being summoned to the Apostle. To make his mind more easily understood, it must be driven home all the more urgently that a woman is bound to her dead husband and cannot take another. Consider: divorce arises from discord, or discord causes it; but death comes by the law of God, not by a man's offense. And death is a debt owed by all, even the unmarried. So if a woman divorced because of discord, anger, hatred, and their causes — injury, insult, or any grievance — is separated in soul and body, she remains bound to her enemy, I will not say her husband; how much more, then, is the woman bound who, neither by her own fault nor her husband's, but by the outcome of the Lord's law, was not severed from marriage but left behind? She will belong to him even in death, the very man to whom she owes concord even now that he is dead. She never heard a repudiation from him; she was never turned away. No certificate of divorce was written for her; she remains with him. She did not want to lose him; she keeps him. She holds the freedom of her mind, which presents to a man everything he lacks as an imaginary fruit. (1 Corinthians 7)

I put the question to the woman herself: Tell me, sister, did you send your husband ahead in peace? What will she answer? Or in discord? Then she is bound to him all the more, because she has a case with him before God. The one who is held back does not depart — but in peace. Therefore she must persevere in that bond with him, since she cannot repudiate him now — not even if she were to marry, had she been able to repudiate him. For indeed she prays for his soul, asks refreshment for him in the meantime, and a share in the first resurrection, and she makes offerings on the annual anniversaries of his death. If she does not do these things, she has truly repudiated him, as far as it lies in her power; and this is all the more unjust, because she could not do it, precisely because she could not; and all the more unworthy, because it is now more unworthy, if she did not deserve it. Or do we suppose we become nothing after death, following some Epicurean rather than Christ? But if we believe the resurrection of the dead, we will surely be held to account, together with those with whom we will rise, to render an account of each other. (1 Corinthians 7)

Even if in that age they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels, that does not mean we will not be held to our deceased spouses, simply because marriage will not be restored. On the contrary, we will be held all the more, because we are destined for a better state: to rise into a spiritual fellowship, recognizing both ourselves and our own. How else will we sing thanks to God for eternity, if the sense and memory of this debt do not remain in us? If we are reformed in substance, not in conscience? Therefore, when we are with God, we will be together — while all of us, with God, are one (though rewards vary, though there are many dwellings with the same Father), having worked for the same wage, namely eternal life, in which God will no more separate those He has joined than He forbids separation in this lesser life. (1 Corinthians 7)

Since this is so, how will she be free for another man, when she is occupied with her own even in the future? We address both sexes, though the speech is directed to one; for a single discipline governs both. Will she have one man in spirit and another in flesh? That would be adultery — the conscience of one woman divided between two men. If the first is separated from the flesh but remains in the heart, there — where even a thought without bodily union perfects adultery from desire, and marriage from will — he is still a husband, possessing that by which he was made, namely the mind. If another dwells in that mind, it is a crime. Yet he is not excluded, if he has departed from the lower commerce of the flesh. The husband is more honored when he has been made purer. (1 Corinthians 7)

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex conditional clauses regarding the woman's status and the theological arguments regarding resurrection and spiritual consortium. Pass A preserves the sense of every clause, and Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that maintains the author's distinctions. Scripture citations (1 Corinthians 7) added in Pass B are appropriate identifications for the Apostle's context mentioned in the text.
